title: Deep Research Agents and Landscape Scans
answer: Deep research agents and landscape scans cover the use of AI systems to carry out multi step literature searches, gather sources, and assemble a structured view of what is known about a topic. crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Deep research agents and landscape scans cover the use of AI systems to carry out multi step literature searches, gather sources, and assemble a structured view of what is known about a topic. A landscape scan is the broader exercise, mapping who works on a problem, which methods dominate, and where evidence is thin, while a deep research agent is the software that automates much of the searching, reading, and summarising. In evidence synthesis this sits upstream of a formal systematic review, and it is used to scope a question, find seed papers, and decide whether a full review is warranted.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These agents run on a large language model as the reasoning core, wrapped in a loop that can call a search API, fetch and parse full texts, and keep notes across many steps. Retrieval usually draws on bibliographic databases, preprint servers, and open access repositories, with a vector index over abstracts and full texts so the agent can find passages rather than whole papers. A library of this kind may hold hundreds of research papers and thousands of extracted claims, and the agent's job is to navigate that material without losing the thread of the original question.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work starts with a question broken into sub questions, then the agent searches, screens titles and abstracts, retrieves full texts, and extracts findings into a table of study, population, method, and result. Each claim is traced back to the sentence and page it came from, so a reviewer can check it rather than trust the summary. Human review remains central: the agent proposes, the reviewer verifies, and disagreements are resolved against the source text. Outputs are typically a narrative map, a evidence table, and a list of gaps, not a finished review.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The main risks are fabricated citations, misread findings, and coverage skewed toward whatever is easiest to retrieve, which can quietly exclude non English or paywalled work. Provenance is the control: every statement should carry a link to the original paper, and content should point to the source rather than to a search tool that sits between the reader and the evidence. Copyright and licence terms govern how much full text can be stored or reproduced, and review protocols, search dates, and inclusion criteria should be recorded so the scan can be repeated. On medical topics the output is a map of the literature, not guidance for any individual's care.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect agents to get better at long horizon tasks, holding a question open across hundreds of sources and updating their map as new papers appear. Benchmarks for citation accuracy and coverage are likely to become standard, and journals and review bodies will push for disclosure of how much of a synthesis was machine assisted. The realistic near term role is a fast first pass that a human then audits, with the agent handling retrieval and extraction while the reviewer owns judgement and interpretation.
